title: Ag Displacement on Cu Foam with Additives for Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide to Carbon Monoxide:
abstract: For electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide, an Ag catalyst supported by Cu foam was prepared electrochemically by bubble-templated Cu electrodeposition and subsequent Ag galvanic displacement. The morphology and crystal structure of the displaced Ag on the Cu foam varied significantly depending on the type of additive. Electrochemical analysis revealed variations in the electrochemical surface area and different Ag and Cu surface compositions depending on the type of additive used in the Ag galvanic displacement step. Among the prepared Ag/Cu foams, the foam having the highest Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio exhibited the highest CO Faradaic efficiency at a certain constant potential. In the potential range between −0.46 and −0.96 VRHE, the Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio significantly affected the normalized CO partial current, showing the importance of control of a certain facet in the Ag crystal structure by the additives.

Ag Displacement on Cu Foam with Additives for Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide to Carbon Monoxide
Hyunju Lee and Sang Hyun Ahn*
School of Chemical Engineering and Material Science, Chung-Ang University, Seoul 06974, Republic of Korea. *E-mail: shahn@cau.ac.kr
Received April 26, 2017, Accepted July 12, 2017, Published online August 24, 2017
For electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide, an Ag catalyst supported by Cu foam was prepared electrochemically by bubble-templated Cu electrodeposition and subsequent Ag galvanic displacement. The morphology and crystal structure of the displaced Ag on the Cu foam varied significantly depending on the type of additive. Electrochemical analysis revealed variations in the electrochemical surface area and different Ag and Cu surface compositions depending on the type of additive used in the Ag galvanic displacement step. Among the prepared Ag/Cu foams, the foam having the highest Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio exhibited the highest CO Faradaic efficiency at a certain constant potential. In the potential range between −0.46 and −0.96 VRHE, the Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio significantly affected the normalized CO partial current, showing the importance of control of a certain facet in the Ag crystal structure by the additives.
Keywords: Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction, Carbon monoxide production, Bubble-templated copper electrodeposition, Silver galvanic displacement, Additive

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
With increasing use of fossil fuels, the emission of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere has increased dramatically, resulting in serious global warming.1,2 To address this environmental problem, various efforts have been made by many research groups to develop technology for converting carbon dioxide to useful products.3–22 In particular, electrochemical conversion of carbon dioxide has received considerable attention because this method, unlike thermochemical conversion, can be used to convert carbon dioxide at room temperature or atmospheric pressure. Furthermore, reuse of the supporting electrolytes facilitates minimal consumption of chemicals.23 However, carbon dioxide is very stable, indicating that an effective catalyst is necessary to relieve the high overpotential for electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide.24 During the last few decades, various electrocatalysts have been investigated depending on the targeted product, for example, methane,3,4 methanol,5,6 formic acid,7–10 and carbon monoxide.11–21 For carbon monoxide production, Ag11–20 and Au21,22 are known to be highly active and selective electrocatalysts. Although Ag is less active and selective than Au, the lower limitation for economic problem facilitates that the Ag becomes a strong candidate for carbon monoxide production. To modify the intrinsic activity of Ag, various strategies have been applied, such as fabrication of Ag–M bimetallic or alloy catalysts (M = Cu, Sn, Zn, etc.)12–15 and oxidederived Ag catalysts.16 Another approach is morphological control of Ag to obtain a large electrochemical surface area (ECSA).17,18 Jiao et al. reported a nanoporous Ag catalyst
with a CO partial current density of −8.1 mA/cm2 and a Faradaic efficiency of approximately 90% at −0.5 VRHE. 11 The high activity and selectivity of nanoporous Ag for CO production were found to originate in certain highly populated facets in the Ag crystal structure.19,20 An additional advantage of roughness-controlled Ag catalysts is the variation in their intrinsic activity depending on the Ag roughness factor.17,18 Surendranath et al. reported that the CO Faradaic efficiency of mesostructured Ag inversed opals increased with increasing roughness factor.18 The maximum CO Faradaic efficiency of approximately 94% at −0.6 VRHE was obtained at a roughness factor of 105, and it decreased to approximately 62% for rougher surfaces. However, roughened Ag catalysts typically require the use of very large amounts of Ag metal, and the cost becomes a serious problem, despite the high performance of the catalyst. Bubble-templated electrodeposition is a promising method of obtaining a large ECSA.25–27 In an aqueous solution containing a metal precursor, the highly negative deposition potential, assisted by hydrogen bubble generation, enables the formation of a porous foam structure. The foam structure can be fabricated by this method in a very short time under ambient pressure and temperature. In addition, the pore size and wall thickness of the foam structure can be easily controlled by varying the electrolyte composition, deposition current, and deposition time. Furthermore, this method can be applied to not only cheap transition metals (Cu, Ni, and Sn) but also expensive noble metals (Au and Ag).25–29 In particular, transition metal foams can provide a large ECSA to support a small amount of a noble metal catalyst that is formed on top of the foam structure.

In electrochemical fabrication processes from Ag ion to Ag metal, the addition of various additives to the aqueous solution significantly affects the morphology and crystal structure of Ag. For example, Koo et al. reported that the addition of 1,2,3-benzotriazole (BTA) to an Ag electrodeposition bath suppressed the formation of Ag(111) structure.30 On the other hand, the growth of Ag(111) structure was accelerated by the addition of polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)31 and 2-nitrobenzoic acid (NA).32 In addition, Lai et al. demonstrated that Ag nanoplates were formed when Ag displacement on a Cu foil substrate was performed with the addition of NA.33
In this study, Ag/Cu foam electrocatalysts were prepared by bubble-templated Cu foam electrodeposition and subsequent Ag galvanic displacement. The large ECSA of the porous Cu foam support provided a number of active sites for Ag galvanic displacement, which minimized the use of precious metals. In the Ag galvanic displacement step, various additives, i.e., BTA, PVP, and NA, were used to form various Ag morphologies and crystal structures. The material properties of the Ag/Cu foams were carefully investigated, and their catalytic activity for electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide was examined.

sections.heading: Experimental
sections.text:
Before Cu electrodeposition, a Ti foil substrate (Sejin, 2 × 2 cm2, thickness: 0.1 mm) was ultrasonicated in 30% ethanol solution for 2 min to remove organic residues. Then the substrate was immersed in a 6 M HCl solution at 70 C for 30 min to eliminate the native oxide. The electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition consisted of 0.12 M CuSO4 5H2O (99.0%, Daejung, Siheung-si, Korea), 0.5 M H2SO4 (95.0%, Junsei, Toyko, Japan), 1.2 M (NH4)2SO4 (99.0%, Alfa Aesar, Haverhill, Massachusetts, USA), and 0.4 mM BTA (98.5%, Daejung).34 Electrodeposition was performed in a conventional three-electrode system composed of the Ti foil as the working electrode, a Pt wire as the counter electrode, and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE, KCl saturated) as the reference electrode. The Ti foil was sealed in a lab-made Teflon cell with an area of 1.13 cm2 exposed to the electrolyte. The Cu foam on the Ti foil substrate was fabricated using two chronopotentiometry steps, at −2.5 mA/cm2 for 60 s and at −1200 mA/cm2 for 40 s, which were controlled using a potentiostat (Autolab PGSTAT302N, Metrohm, Herisau, Swiss). After careful washing with deionized water, the Cu foam was immersed in an Ag displacement solution consisting of 0.05 M AgNO3 (99.9%, Alfa Aesar), 0.5 M (NH4)2SO4 (99.0%, Alfa Aesar), and 3.5 M NH4OH (28.0%, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, Missouri, USA) for 10 min at room temperature.35 Ag displacement was conducted without and with the additives BTA (98.5%, Daejung), PVP (average mol. wt. 40 000, Sigma-Aldrich), and NA (95%, SigmaAldrich). All the electrolytes used to fabricate the Ag/Cu
foams were purged by N2 gas (99.995%) flow for 30 min before the experiments. To image the morphologies of the Ag/Cu foams, field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, SIGMA, Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) was used. The crystal structure was analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, New D8 Advance, Bruker-AXS, Billerica, Massachusetts, USA). The surface properties of the Ag/Cu foams were investigated using anodic scans in linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in a 0.1 M KOH solution at a scan rate of 1 mV/s. Electrochemical CO2 conversion by the Ag/Cu foams was performed using an H-type cell (Pine Research Instrumentation, Durham, North Carolina, USA). The cell capacity was 25 mL for both the cathode and anode parts, which were separated by a proton-conducting membrane (Nafion, Wilmington, Delaware, USA NRE-212). The cathode part contained an Ag/Cu foam as a working electrode and an SCE as a reference electrode. The exposed area of the working electrode was fixed at 0.5 cm2. The anode part contained Pt gauze as a counter electrode. KHCO3 (99.5%, Daejung, 0.1 M) at a pH of 6.8 was used for both the catholyte and anolyte, which were purged by N2 gas for 30 min. Then, the catholyte was purged by CO2 gas (99.995%) at a rate of 300 sccm for at least 45 min before the activity measurement. To maintain CO2 saturation during the experiment, CO2 gas was continuously injected into the catholyte at a rate of 10 sccm, ensuring that the product gases entered the sampling loop for gas chromatography (GC, Agilent 7890A). The chronoamperometry method was adopted to analyze the catalytic activity of the Ag/Cu foams at various potentials for 30 min. The CO concentration generated at the cathode was measured by a flame ionization detector (FID) in the GC instrument. Then, the CO Faradaic efficiency was obtained by calculating the concentration of generated CO and the amount of electrochemically applied charge.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 1(a) shows the results of chronopotentiometry performed by galvanostatic two-step electrodeposition to fabricate the Cu foam on a Ti foil substrate. To increase the adhesion between the substrate and electrodeposited Cu, a low current density of −2.5 mA/cm2 was applied for 60 s. After the first step, Cu particles approximately 2 μm in size appeared on the surface of Ti foil substrate, as shown in Figure 1(b). Then, the Cu foam was electrodeposited using a high current density of −1200 mA/cm2 for 40 s, as shown in Figure 1(c). The Cu electrodeposition at a high current density was accompanied by vigorous generation of hydrogen bubbles, facilitating the formation of Cu foams with a large surface area.25 The observed pore size and wall thickness of the Cu foam were 64.8 13.6 μm and 15.1 5.9 μm, respectively. The Ag/Cu foams were prepared by Cu electrodeposition and subsequent Ag displacement for 10 min without or with an additive. Ag can be displaced spontaneously on Cu

After the displacement, the branch of Cu foam disappeared while the much smoother foams with round pores were observed as shown in Figure 2, indicating the Ag formation on the surface of Cu foam.36 Figure 2(a) shows FESEM images of the Ag/Cu foam prepared using an additive-free Ag solution consisting of 0.05 M AgNO3, 0.5 M (NH4)2SO4, and 3.5 M NH4OH (Ag/CF). The pore size was approximately 56.3 2.6 μm, and the wall thickness was 20.4 3.5 μm. The high-magnification image in the inset shows the formation of agglomerated Ag spheres, which clearly differed from the Cu foam morphology (Figure 1(c)). Figure 2 (b) shows FESEM images of the Ag/Cu foam prepared by adding 1 mM BTA to the Ag electrodeposition solution (Ag/CF-BTA). The pore size (41.6 10.3 μm) and wall thickness (17.5 7.8 μm) were both smaller than those of Ag/CF. The inset image shows significant agglomeration of
round Ag particles. Figure 2(c) shows the Ag/Cu foam prepared by adding 1 mM PVP to the electrodeposition solution (Ag/CF-PVP). The pore size was 39.3 8.0 μm, and the wall thickness was 15.6 4.4 μm, which were also smaller than those of Ag/CF. The Ag particles were obviously smaller than those in Ag/CF because the PVP acted as a capping agent, suppressing the growth of Ag particles.37 Figure 2(d) shows the Ag/Cu foam prepared by adding 1 mM NA to the Ag electrodeposition bath (Ag/CFNA). The pore size and wall thickness of Ag/CF-NA were 35.1 7.5 μm and 18.5 5.3 μm, respectively. The addition of NA as a complexing agent controlling the morphology of Ag produced agglomerated Ag plates (inset of Figure 2(d)), in good agreement with a previous report.33 In addition, molecular dynamics simulations have revealed selective adsorption of NA additive on Ag(111) rather than Ag(100) and Ag(110).33
Figure 3(a) shows the XRD patterns of the Ti foil substrate, Cu foam, and Ag/Cu foam samples with various additives. The Ti foil showed the (100), (002), (101), (102), (110), and (103) peaks of Ti metal [JCPDS no. 44-1294]. After the Cu foam formed on the Ti foil, the intensity of the Ti metal peaks decreased, and three Cu metal peaks appeared at 43.3 (111), 50.4 (200), and 74.1 (220) [JCPDS no. 04-0836]. After Ag displacement without an additive (Ag/CF), Ag metallic peaks were observed at

However, the intensity ratio of Ag(220)/Ag(111) for Ag/CF-BTA was higher than that for Ag/CF, in agreement with a previous result.30 For Ag/CFPVP, the Ag(111) intensity was obviously larger than that for Ag/CF; PVP is known to be selectively adsorbed on Ag(111).31 A further increase in Ag(111) was observed for Ag/CF-NA. This result was also in good agreement with a previous report.32 The XRD analysis indicated that the crystal structure of displaced Ag on the Cu foam was significantly affected by the type of additive. To investigate the electrochemical behavior, LSV measurements were conducted in N2-purged 0.1 M KOH at a scan rate of 1 mV/s. As shown in Figure 4(a), several anodic peaks were observed. The first anodic peak (A1) in the potential range of 0.45–0.80 VRHE could be assigned to oxidation of
Cu0 to Cu1+ (2Cu + 2OH− ! Cu2O + H2O + 2e−).38 The A2 and A3 peaks, in the potential range of 0.80–1.10 VRHE, demonstrated further oxidation of Cu2O to CuO (2Cu2O + 2 OH− ! 2CuO + H2O + 2e−).38 The charge densities of the sum of the two peaks (A2 + A3) for the Ag/Cu foam samples were in the order Ag/CF-BTA > Ag/CF-NA > Ag/CF-PVP > Ag/CF. Peaks A4–A6 in the potential range of 1.12–1.55 VRHE could be identified as representing the oxidation of Ag 0 to Ag1+ (2Ag + 2OH− ! Ag2O + H2O + 2e−).38 Then further oxidation of Ag2O to AgO was represented by the A7 peak (Ag2O + 2OH
− ! 2AgO + H2O + 2e−).38 The charge densities of the samples are summarized in Figure 4(b). The calculated ratio between CuO and AgO formation in Figure 4 (b) demonstrated that the ratio of AgO formation for Ag/CF was much higher than that for other Ag/CFs with additives. This result shows that the kinetics of Ag displacement was faster without the additives than with them, indicating that adsorption of additives on the displaced Ag suppressed the rate of Ag displacement. The ratio of charge densities for AgO/CuO formation was in the following order: Ag/CF > Ag/CF-NA ≥ Ag/CF-PVP > Ag/CF-BTA. At potentials more

Figure 5(a) shows the chronoamperometry results for the prepared Ag/Cu foam samples without and with additives in CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 at −0.66 VRHE for 1800 s. After about 600 s, the current densities for electrochemical CO2 reduction were generally stabilized. In the analytic range between 1740 and 1800 s, the calculated charge densities were in the order Ag/CF-NA > Ag/CF > Ag/CF-PVP > Ag/ CF-BTA, as demonstrated in the inset of Figure 5(a). On the basis of the CO concentration detected by the FID column in GC, the Faradaic efficiency for CO production was obtained, as shown in Figure 5(b). The CO Faradaic efficiency of Ag/CF was 9.8% at the Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio of 0.134 calculated from XRD analysis (Figure 3(b)). As the Ag(220)/ Ag(111) ratio increased from 0.134 to 0.228, the CO Faradaic efficiency increased from 9.8 to 17.8%. The lower CO Faradaic efficiency compared with a previous study using a Ag catalyst11–20 might originate from the exposed area of Cu that was not displaced by Ag, indicating that an increase in the Ag surface, which affects the Ag displacement process, can be expected to yield higher CO Faradaic efficiency. Furthermore, the CO partial current density normalized using the charge density of AgO formation (Figure 4(b)) also increased with increasing Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio. The highest CO Faradaic efficiency and normalized CO partial current density were obtained for the Ag/CF-BTA catalyst, which had the highest Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio. This relationship is in good agreement with a previous result showing that Ag(220) demonstrates higher selectivity to CO generation than other Ag crystal facets.20
The normalized CO partial current densities of various Ag/Cu foams without and with the additives were obtained in the potential range between −0.46 and −0.96 VRHE at 0.10 V intervals. As shown in Figure 6, Ag/CF exhibited normalized CO partial current densities of −0.045 to −0.075 mA/CAg. The values for both Ag/CF-PVP and
Ag/CF-NA were slightly enhanced. However, Ag/CF-BTA exhibited significant improvement in the normalized CO partial current density compared with Ag/CF in the entire potential range. Notably, at −0.96 VRHE, the value was 3.7 times higher than that of Ag/CF. As mentioned above, the highly populated Ag(220) facets facilitated the high activity of the Ag/CF-BTA catalyst for CO production by electrochemical CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
Bubble-templated Cu electrodeposition and subsequent Ag galvanic displacement facilitated the successful fabrication of various Ag/Cu foam samples to obtain a large ECSA as well as low Ag loading. FESEM analysis confirmed that the foam structure of the electrodeposited Cu was maintained after Ag galvanic displacement, and Ag/Cu foam samples with various surface morphologies were obtained according to the absence or presence of the additives BTA, PVP, or NA. XRD analysis indicated that the displaced Ag had polycrystalline crystal structures, and the ratios of Ag(111), (200), and (220) varied depending on the type of additive. Electrochemical analysis demonstrated that the surface composition of Ag and Cu was also affected by the type of additive. For electrochemical CO2 reduction at a constant potential of −0.66 VRHE, the calculated CO Faradaic efficiency of Ag/CF-BTA was 1.8 times higher than that of Ag/CF. The enhancement can be attributed to the fact that Ag/CF-BTA had the highest Ag(220)/Ag(111) ratio among the Ag/Cu foam samples. In the potential range of −0.46 to −0.96 VRHE, Ag/CF-BTA showed the highest CO partial current normalized by the charge for AgO formation owing to the highly populated Ag(220) facets.
